public_summary: Jungle Chess played with the solar system. Every piece is a planet, and a planet's size on the board is the fifth root of its real measured diameter, so rank is something you can see rather than something you have to learn: Mercury is the smallest world in play and Jupiter the largest, and the traditional rules are followed exactly as written. Matter faces antimatter. One army's worlds lean their poles one way and the other army's lean the other, by each planet's own true axial tilt, and the bases give the same answer again in white against black. Four of the eight worlds wear a real map: Earth its own coastlines, Mars its own dark continents, Mercury its smooth plains with the Caloris basin in them, and Venus -- alone in the set -- a surface no eye has ever seen, the Magellan radar map, still upside down because Venus's axis is tipped 177 degrees. The other four wear their weather. Saturn is the world this edition corrects, and it is the only correction in the chain that takes something away. It used to wear four identical brown bands, evenly spaced, in the loudest pair of colours in the box; its own reference is the softest picture in the set. So the bands came down in tone rather than up: five of them now, nine, fifteen, eight, sixteen and twelve degrees wide, unevenly spaced and not symmetric about the equator, four in a mid amber and only the widest still brown, the two widest slightly wavy rather than exact circles, and a bright cap above fifty-eight degrees north in the ring's own white. The ring itself did not move. Next to Jupiter, loud on purpose on the same board, Saturn is now the quiet one. A cocoa-brown asteroid belt crosses the middle of the field, a star stands at each end with two flames bursting off the board edge, and the three cells around each star are sunken corona wells where a captured world drops out of the light and its rank counts for nothing. You win by walking one of your worlds onto the rival star.
